chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Hammad, from Hariz, who said: Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said to Zurara and Muhammad ibn Muslim:

The milk, and the colostrum, and the egg, and the hair, and the wool, and the horn, and the tooth, and the hoof, and everything separated from the sheep and the riding animal — it is ritually pure (zakiy).
But if you take it from the animal after it has died, wash it and pray in it.

key_terms.الدابة: Dabbah — a riding/pack animal, used broadly for horses, donkeys, mules and similar beasts of burden
key_terms.اللبأ: Colostrum — the first milk produced after birth, sometimes treated differently from regular milk in jurisprudence
key_terms.ذكي: Zakiy — ritually pure; in jurisprudential usage refers to something that is clean/permissible, especially products from animals. Derived from the concept of tazkiyah (purification).

ai.seo_question: Are animal products like milk, wool, and eggs ritually pure in Islamic jurisprudence?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) issued this legal ruling to two of his most learned companions, Zurara and Muhammad ibn Muslim, who were leading jurists of the Shia community. The ruling establishes that natural products and body parts separated from living animals (milk, colostrum, eggs, hair, wool, horns, teeth, hooves) are ritually pure and may be used in prayer. However, if such items are taken from an animal after it has died (and thus becomes a carcass, najis), they must be washed before prayer can be performed while wearing them. This reflects the jurisprudential principle that the state of the animal at the time of separation determines the ruling.
